statements.markdown:
Here is the elementary calculus step. Suppose
$q\in C^1([r,1))$, $q(r)=r$, $q'(r)\le1$, $q\le1$, and $q'$
is strictly convex on $(r,1)$. If $q(t)\ge t$ at some $r<t<1$,
strict integration below the finite endpoint chord gives
$$
t-r\le\int_r^t q'(v)\,dv
 <\frac{t-r}{2}\bigl(q'(r)+q'(t)\bigr),
$$
so $q'(t)>1$. For $t<s<1$, convexity then gives
$$
q'(s)\ge q'(t)+\frac{s-t}{t-r}\bigl(q'(t)-q'(r)\bigr)
\ge q'(t)>1.
$$
Consequently $q(s)\ge t+(s-t)q'(t)>1$ for $s$ sufficiently
close to one, a contradiction. Thus $q(t)<t$ throughout $(r,1)$.
All chord endpoints lie below one; no derivative at one is used.
statements.section: 5. Excluding terminal, interior and initial gaps

statements.markdown:
A terminal gap $(r,1)$ with nonempty support has $r\in S$ and
positive plateau height. Suppose $q(t)\geq t$ for some $r<t<1$.
Strict convexity of $q'$ and $q'(r)\leq1$ give
$$
t-r\leq\int_r^t q'(s)\,ds
<\frac{t-r}{2}\bigl(q'(r)+q'(t)\bigr),
$$
so $q'(t)>1$. Convexity then gives $q'(s)>q'(t)>1$ for $s>t$.
Consequently $q(s)>t+(s-t)q'(t)>1$ for $s<1$ sufficiently
close to one, contrary to $q\leq1$. Thus $q(t)<t$ on $(r,1)$,
and $G(r)<0$ contradicts minimality. This uses no contact at one.
statements.section: 2. Minimality gives contact; curvature excludes gaps

statements.markdown:
**Reaching the diagonal forces a slope above one.**
Put $h(t)=q'(t)-1$, so $h(r)\le0$. If $q(t)\ge t$ at some
$r<t<1$, strict integration below the chord on the finite interval
$[r,t]$ would give

$$
0\le q(t)-t=\int_r^t h(v)\,dv
<\frac{t-r}{2}\bigl(h(r)+h(t)\bigr)
\le\frac{t-r}{2}h(t).
$$

Hence $h(t)>0$.

**The excess slope persists and violates the bound.**
To control a later slope, use the same chord rule
on the larger interval $[r,s]$, where $t<s<1$. At its interior
point $t$ this gives

$$
h(t)\le\frac{s-t}{s-r}h(r)+\frac{t-r}{s-r}h(s).
$$

Solving for the right endpoint gives

$$
h(s)\ge h(t)+\frac{s-t}{t-r}\bigl(h(t)-h(r)\bigr)\ge h(t)>0.
$$

The bound holds at every time after $t$, so integration gives
$q(s)\ge t+(s-t)(1+h(t))$. Choose any time

$$
t+\frac{1-t}{1+h(t)}<s<1.
$$

Such a choice exists because $h(t)>0$, and the lower bound now gives
$q(s)>1$, contradicting $q(s)\le1$ strictly before time one.
Thus $q(t)<t$ throughout $(r,1)$, giving
$G(r)=\int_r^1(q(t)-t)\,dt<0$, contrary to the addition test.

statements.markdown:
**[Question 4](#question-4).** Set $h=q'-1$. Since $q(r)=r$, reaching or passing the diagonal at
$t$ means $\int_r^t h\ge0$. Strict convexity places $h$ below its
endpoint chord, so that integral is less than
$(t-r)(h(r)+h(t))/2$. With $h(r)\le0$, this forces $h(t)>0$.
The chord rule on $[r,s]$, solved for $h(s)$, keeps every later value
at least $h(t)$. Integrating gives
$q(s)\ge t+(s-t)(1+h(t))>1$ for a suitable $s<1$, violating the
bound. If $q$ never reaches the diagonal, then $G(r)<0$ instead.
Thus both possibilities contradict the conditions on a minimiser.
statements.note: This repeats the chord proof of Section 5.4, which the support model does not use and the scalar contact proof does.

statements.markdown:
For the proposed polynomial, $q(0)=0$, $q'(0)=1$, $q'''=6>0$, and
direct integration gives $G(s)=s^3(1-s)/4\ge0$, with $G(0)=0$.
Its derivative has minimum $13/16$, so $q$ increases to $5/4$ as
$t\uparrow1$. It is bounded, but $q(9/10)=2043/2000>1$.
The other reduced conditions therefore do not replace the exact cap
supplied by $|u|\le1$.
